llama3.2:3b has a strong position bias.** Its verdict flipped in 18 of 40 pairs when the two answers swapped places, and it preferred whichever answer came first 72% of the time. [1] llama3.2:3b | 55% | 72% | 70% | 45% [3]

The two models barely agree with each other:** Cohen's κ = 0.21 ("fair") on the 30 non-gold pairs, Krippendorff's α = 0.19. [3] Raters see a prompt and two responses, judge them against a rubric, and pick the better one on a 5-point scale. [1]

DPO JSONL (`prompt`, `chosen`, `rejected`, `meta`) in the format TRL's `DPOTrainer` reads, with filters for minimum labels, agreement and margin (to drop near-ties) and for excluding raters. [1] The app tracks how much raters agree, flags unreliable raters, and exports clean `{prompt, chosen, rejected}` pairs ready for training. [2]

Labeling teams handle this with overlap (several raters per pair), gold questions with known answers, and agreement statistics. [1] To check that the agreement metrics behave correctly, [`scripts/simulate_raters.py`](scripts/simulate_raters.py) gives 400 pairs a hidden true score and simulates three raters who report it with a given probability ("skill") and guess randomly otherwise. [2]

A single rater clicking quickly, a rater who always picks whichever answer is on the left, or a rubric nobody reads can quietly poison a dataset. [1] A simulated rater who guesses "left" whenever unsure is caught by the position-bias metric: they pick the left side 76% of the time, versus 51% for careful raters. [2]
